title: How the Human Microbiome Project Works
summary: Josh and Chuck explore the Human Microbiome Project, launched by the National Institutes of Health in 2007 to map the microbes living in and on the human body. They cover how microbes outnumber human cells, the roles of gut bacteria in digestion, mood (serotonin), vitamin synthesis, immunity, allergies, obesity and possibly cancer, and how metagenomics made the study possible. They note that no single baseline healthy microbiome exists, that everyone's microbiome is individual, and that probiotics and antibiotics raise open questions. The episode includes a sponsor read for NatureBox, and closes with a listener email from a creationist biologist named Eric from South Bend, Indiana, about the overlap between creationism and evolution.

segments.title: Opening banter and gut-mood connection
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck open with small talk about an IKEA lamp commercial, then introduce the idea that gut health affects mood, since most serotonin is produced in the gut through the microbiome.

segments.title: Microbes in the body and the tree of life
segments.summary: The hosts discuss how the three domains and kingdoms of life were classified, how archaea differ from bacteria, and the scale of microbes in the body, including that microbial genes outnumber human genes and microbes outweigh a few pounds of body mass.

segments.title: Balance of microbes: viruses, lions and gazelles
segments.summary: The hosts explain that many microbes, including some considered harmful like E. coli, live in balance; viruses in the microbiome keep bacterial populations in check, and disease tends to occur when the microbiome gets out of balance. Chuck and Josh also note that about a third to half of stool is microbial biomass.

segments.title: NatureBox sponsor read
segments.summary: Sponsor read for NatureBox, a subscription snack service, with a discount offer for listeners.

segments.title: Human Microbiome Project origins and metagenomics
segments.summary: The NIH launched the Human Microbiome Project in 2007 to map the microbiome, aiming to establish a baseline healthy microbiome; a University of Michigan finding suggests no single baseline exists. The hosts explain metagenomics, which allows scientists to sample and study microbes directly rather than only culturing lab-friendly species.

segments.title: Findings: gum disease, probiotics, obesity, infancy and immunity
segments.summary: The hosts discuss findings including bacteria linked to gum disease and cavities (Streptococcus mutans), uncertainty about probiotics, gut bacteria and obesity in mice, a bacterium that helps infants digest breast milk acquired during birth, and the microbiome's role in training the immune system. They tie this to the hygiene hypothesis and allergies.

segments.title: Personalized medicine and microbiome links to cancer
segments.summary: The hosts discuss that everyone's microbiome is different, pointing toward personalized medicine, and mention reported links between certain cancers and bacteria. They also suggest a future episode on the microbiome.

segments.title: Listener mail from a creationist biologist
segments.summary: Josh reads an email from Eric in South Bend, Indiana, a Christian biologist and creationist who says creationists accept microevolution and natural selection but differ on the age of Earth and the origin of species.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts thank listeners and invite contact through social media, email, and the website.
